sentences.text: Baurusuchus was a land-dwelling meat-eater that grew to lengths of 3.5 to 4 meters and could weigh as much as 113.4 kilograms.
Its skull was laterally compressed and its teeth were shaped similarly to those of theropod dinosaurs, rather than resembling modern crocodilians.
Despite its size, this predator generated a bite force between 2542 and 3088 Newtons, a strength comparable to that of an American alligator.
It likely hunted by ambushing prey and pulling it back with serrated, blade-like teeth in a manner similar to a Komodo dragon.
The genus was first described by Price in 1945, with the authority for the name attributed to him in that year.
Three species are known: Baurusuchus pachecoi, named by Price in 1945; Baurusuchus salgadoensis, named by Carvalho et al. in 2005; and Baurusuchus albertoi, named by Nascimento and Zaher in 2010.
Enlarged and strongly bent pterygoids allowed the animal to close its jaw very quickly, although this rapid bite was somewhat weak.
The animal may have shaken prey violently with its jaws, aided by enlarged cervical neural spines that served as large muscle anchors.
Like modern alligators, Baurusuchus likely dug holes to find water during dry seasons or for thermoregulation.
It likely competed with abelisaurid dinosaurs for food in its ecosystem.
Baurusuchus is the type genus of the family Baurusuchidae, which includes crocodiliforms with elongated and laterally compressed skulls.
A 2011 study established a new subfamily called Baurusuchinae, which serves as the parent group for Baurusuchus.

This subfamily includes only Stratiotosuchus and Baurusuchus, making Stratiotosuchus the closest known relative, while a 2014 study supported a closer relationship between them than with Aplestosuchus.
Baurusuchus lived in Brazil between 90 and 83.5 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous period in a hot and arid climate.
Its time range extended from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian stages, between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.

Some researchers do not support the affiliation of Baurusuchus albertoi to Baurusuchus, viewing it instead as a close relative of Aplestosuchus, a view supported by a study that considers it an exception to the genus.
